2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable (no longitudinal participant follow-up); however, substantial administrative item missingness is present in DataSUS SIM mortality records, where 23% of 1996-2014 DRSAI deaths lacked race/color classification (PDF pp. 13-14).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern (weak control): Although poverty, regional/spatial segregation, urban vs. rural/traditional settlement, nutrition, and age are discussed narratively (PDF pp. 6-11, 13, 17), the empirical analysis presents unadjusted national bivariate shares without stratification, age standardization, or multivariable adjustment for socioeconomic or geographic confounders.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate (qualitative doctrinal-historical operationalization): Accurately cites Brazil's 1988 Federal Constitution (arts. 196, 200, 225), Basic Sanitation Law No. 11.445/2007, Statute of Racial Equality Law No. 12.288/2010, and the 2013 National Policy for Holistic Health of the Black Population (PNSIPN) (PDF pp. 3, 7, 11), analyzing non-enforcement as institutional/environmental racism, but does not measure legal implementation or enforcement quantitatively across jurisdictions.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern: Household sanitation deficits (2010 IBGE Census) and DRSAI mortality (1996-2014 DataSUS SIM) use official national definitions, but DRSAI deaths suffer from underreporting and 23% missing race/color records, comparisons rely on raw counts/compositional proportions rather than population- or age-standardized rates, and 2008-2016 hospitalization totals lack exact ICD-10 specifications (PDF pp. 11-15).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate: Clearly defines four household basic sanitation inadequacy indicators from the 2010 IBGE Census (lack of water supply, waste collection, sewage treatment, and household bathroom; PDF pp. 11-12, Figure 1) and enumerates the specific infectious and parasitic diseases included in 1996-2014 DataSUS DRSAI mortality (Footnotes 9-10, PDF pp. 9, 13, Figure 2), though per-capita/age-adjusted rates and exact ICD-10 codes are omitted.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: No pre-analysis plan or systematic search protocol exists; exploratory bibliographic synthesis carries risk of selective source selection, minor citation inconsistencies appear (e.g., DataSUS cited as Brasil 2006 on p. 13 vs. Brasil 2016 on p. 14), and Indigenous/Asian categories are omitted from Figures 1-2, though missing DataSUS racial data are transparently reported (PDF pp. 4, 7, 12-14).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: The historical-theoretical component uses non-systematic exploratory bibliographic selection (Gil 2009; PDF p. 5) without search strings or inclusion criteria; the empirical component uses national census/administrative registries but excludes Indigenous and Asian-descent categories from comparative charts and faces 23% missing race/color classification in DataSUS mortality records (PDF pp. 11-14).

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: This paper (an English translation in Simbiótica 2026 of an article originally published in Saúde e Sociedade in 2020) is a political-historical and doctrinal-empirical hybrid study examining environmental and institutional racism in Brazilian sanitation and health from the colonial period to contemporary constitutional governance. Because it combines doctrinal/policy and historical synthesis ('exploratory-level bibliographic research according to Gil, 2009') with descriptive secondary tabulations of national administrative and census databases (IBGE 2010 Demographic Census housing/sanitation deficits and Tabnet DataSUS 1996-2014 SIM mortality and 2008-2016 SIH hospitalizations for Diseases Related to Inadequate Environmental Sanitation [DRSAI]), it fits the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework rather than a systematic review tool (AMSTAR 2), a primary qualitative fieldwork checklist (CASP), or an individual-level analytical cross-sectional regression checklist (JBI). Under a structured non-validated judgment, the study demonstrates strong legal source accuracy (1988 Federal Constitution arts. 196, 200, 225; Law 11.445/2007; Law 12.288/2010; PNSIPN 2013), jurisdictional specificity, rich historical-institutional contextualization, explicit DRSAI and Census outcome definitions, and unusually candid researcher reflexivity. Conversely, it exhibits weak causal identification, confounding control, selection process, and coding transparency: bibliographic selection is non-systematic, quantitative analyses present unadjusted national compositional shares without age, income, urban/rural, or regional standardization, 23% of DataSUS DRSAI death records lack race/color identification, Indigenous and Asian-descent groups are omitted from comparative charts, and exact ICD-10 and IBGE variable coding scripts are not archived. As the author explicitly acknowledges in the Final Considerations (PDF p. 18), the analysis serves as a macro-level exploratory framing calling for deeper local/comparative quantitative and qualitative research rather than a causally identified policy evaluation.
raw_response.overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: Moderate-to-high methodological concern for causal/epidemiological inference, alongside strong legal-institutional contextualization and reflexivity (4 strong, 4 adequate, 5 weak domains; no numeric composite score computed).
raw_response.study_design_identified: Political-historical and doctrinal-empirical hybrid study combining exploratory bibliographic/legal-policy analysis with descriptive secondary analysis of national census (IBGE 2010) and administrative health data (Tabnet DataSUS SIM 1996-2014 and SIH 2008-2016)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Study aims, researcher reflexivity, and methods ('exploratory-level bibliographic research according to Gil (2009)' plus IBGE 2010 Census and Tabnet DataSUS analysis) are on PDF pp. 1, 3-5; constitutional and statutory frameworks (1988 Constitution, Law 11.445/2007, Law 12.288/2010, PNSIPN 2013) are on PDF pp. 3, 7, 11, 18-19; colonial historiography and DRSAI definitions (Footnotes 9-10) are on PDF pp. 9-11, 13; 2010 Census and 1996-2014 / 2008-2016 DataSUS empirical findings and missing-data caveats are on PDF pp. 11-15 (Figures 1-2); IBGE technician statistical collaboration and data-availability statements are on PDF pp. 22-23.
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The paper is neither a systematic review (explicitly using non-systematic 'exploratory-level bibliographic research according to Gil (2009)', ruling out AMSTAR 2), nor a pure non-empirical essay (ruling out NONE, as it empirically analyzes national 2010 IBGE Census sanitation microdata/tabulations and 1996-2014 / 2008-2016 DataSUS mortality and hospitalization records), nor an analytical cross-sectional survey/regression linking individual or ecological exposures to outcomes within a single sample (ruling out JBI Cross-Sectional, as Census sanitation shares and multi-year DataSUS vital statistics come from separate aggregate national registries without linked analytical modeling). Instead, it is a doctrinal/policy and historical-institutional case study of Brazilian sanitation law and institutional racism integrated with descriptive national administrative evidence, matching the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework.
